userJob: Place design tokens so every route can read them
problem: Tokens are declared in a CSS module, so their properties are scoped to the element the hashed class lands on and any component rendered above it has no tokens at all
worksWhen: Any Next.js build using the App Router
avoidWhen: The project already routes tokens through a Tailwind theme layer, where adding a second declaration is the drift
mechanism: Declare tokens once in the global stylesheet the root layout imports. If Tailwind is installed, the tokens belong to its theme layer and classes reference them. Two systems naming the same value is drift you debug later, so pick the one the project already uses.
risks: A module-scoped token block that works on the page it was written for and nowhere else
Duplicating a value in both the stylesheet and the Tailwind theme, so half the components move when one is changed
mobileRules: Fluid token values need checking at 375px against the rendered result rather than the declared clamp
accessibilityRules: Colour tokens for both schemes are declared together so the dark scheme is measured rather than inferred
genericnessNote: Token location is a mechanical decision with no design content.

userJob: Decide which components run in the browser
problem: The client directive is placed on a layout to make one interactive child work, so every route beneath it ships to the browser and the layout's metadata export is dropped with no error
worksWhen: Any App Router build with interactive elements
avoidWhen: The Pages Router, where none of this applies and the wrapper is a different file entirely
mechanism: Server is the default. Put the client directive on the leaf that needs state or an event handler, never on a layout, because it is inherited. Check for a pages directory first: if the routes are there, this is the Pages Router and the layout, head and metadata rules are different.
risks: A silently dropped metadata export, which fails no build and shows up as missing page titles
A whole route subtree shipped to the browser because one button needed state
mobileRules: An oversized client bundle costs most on a phone, where the first paint is already the slowest
accessibilityRules: Interactive leaves are where focus management lives; pushing the boundary up does not move the responsibility
genericnessNote: Rendering boundaries are architecture and carry no visual signature.

userJob: Load a typeface in Next.js without buying a layout shift
problem: The face is linked from a font host, so it is discovered late, is not self-hosted, and has no metric-matched fallback, which shows as a shift on first paint
worksWhen: Any Next.js build with a custom typeface
avoidWhen: A face the client self-hosts under their own licence with their own loading strategy
mechanism: Load the face through the framework's font module, called at module scope in the layout and applied as a class. It self-hosts the file and emits a metric-matched fallback, which is the part a link tag cannot provide.
risks: Calling the loader inside a component, which defeats the module-scope requirement
Loading several weights that the type scale never uses
mobileRules: The shift from a late face rewraps every line at 375px, which is where it is most visible
accessibilityRules: Confirm the loaded weights exist in the face; a synthesised weight renders thinner and loses contrast
genericnessNote: A loading mechanism does not choose the face.

userJob: Capture screenshots of a Next.js site that show the page rather than the compiler
problem: The development server compiles on first request, so the first capture of each route is a screenshot of a page that is still being built
worksWhen: Any verification pass against the development server
avoidWhen: A production build served by the production server, where the compile has already happened
mechanism: Request every route once before the render matrix runs. Capture against the development server on its own port. Optimised images are only served by a running server, so the asset manifest records the optimiser's request URLs rather than the paths under the public directory.
risks: A capture that looks broken and is only uncompiled, which sends the run into fixing a design that is fine
Running the matrix against static file paths and concluding the images are missing
mobileRules: Warm the routes once per viewport if the route renders differently by width
accessibilityRules: Automated checks against an uncompiled page report absences that do not exist, so warming is a precondition for trusting the results
genericnessNote: A capture procedure has no design content.

userJob: Recognise the three Next.js failures that look like design problems
problem: A page renders correctly and the markup you inspected is gone, an image collapses to nothing, or every image on a route returns an error, and each of them looks like a styling bug
worksWhen: Diagnosing a Next.js page that renders differently than the source suggests
avoidWhen: Never; these three account for a large share of the stack's confusing symptoms
mechanism: A date, a random value or anything read from the window renders on the server and again on the client, mismatches, and the server HTML is discarded silently. An optimised image without width and height, or filling a parent with no height, collapses to nothing. A remote image host missing from the configured patterns returns an error for every image on the route. The development server also tolerates what the production build refuses, so run the build once before calling a page finished.
risks: Fixing the symptom in CSS, which leaves the mismatch in place to recur
Shipping a page that only the development server accepts
mobileRules: A collapsed image is easier to miss at 375px where the layout is a single column and the gap reads as spacing
accessibilityRules: Discarded server HTML takes its heading structure and landmarks with it, so an accessibility pass on the server output proves nothing about what the user gets
genericnessNote: These are recorded platform failures, not design guidance.
